title: Rational conjugation representation on linear Hom
statement:
Let $k$ be a field [def-weil-field] and $G$ an affine group scheme over $k$ [def-sc-group-scheme]. Put $C=k[G]$, so $G=\operatorname{Spec}C$ [def-weil-affine-spectrum], with comultiplication $\Delta$ and counit $\epsilon$ induced by the group laws. A rational $G$-module means a $k$-vector space $M$ and a $k$-linear coaction $\rho_M:M\to M\otimes_k C$ [def-weil-pbc-module-tensor-product] such that $(\rho_M\otimes1)\rho_M=(1\otimes\Delta)\rho_M$ and $(1\otimes\epsilon)\rho_M=1_M$. For any two finite-dimensional rational $G$-modules $V,W$, the vector space $H=\operatorname{Hom}_k(V,W)$ has a rational $G$-module structure whose action, after every commutative $k$-algebra extension $A$, is
$$(g\cdot f)(v)=g\cdot f(g^{-1}\cdot v)\qquad(g\in G(A),\ f\in H\otimes_k A=\operatorname{Hom}_A(V\otimes_k A,W\otimes_k A),\ v\in V\otimes_k A).$$
For $f\in H$, its coaction satisfies $\rho_H(f)=f\otimes1$ if and only if $f$ is equivariant, meaning $\rho_W f=(f\otimes1)\rho_V$, equivalently $f_A(gv)=g f_A(v)$ for every $A,g,v$ as above. No assumption of smoothness, reducedness, characteristic zero, or algebraic closedness is imposed. Scalar extensions and their induced maps have the meaning in [def-weil-module-base-change].

source.place: Chapter 4, section a, Remark 4.1, printed pp.83-84 (representations and coactions); Lemma 22.40 (b) to (a), printed p.477 (natural G-module Hom and fixed maps).

proof.text: Put $V_A=V\otimes_k A$ and $W_A=W\otimes_k A$. The map $j_A:H\otimes_k A\to\operatorname{Hom}_A(V_A,W_A)$ sends $f\otimes a$ to $(v\otimes b\mapsto f(v)\otimes ab)$. Here is its inverse explicitly. Choose finite bases $(e_i)$ of $V$ and $(w_j)$ of $W$, and let $E_{ji}(e_l)=\delta_{il}w_j$. The scalar-extended bases have coordinate maps $e_i^*\otimes1$, $w_j^*\otimes1$; their expansion identities follow by extending $v=\sum_i e_i e_i^*(v)$ and $w=\sum_j w_j w_j^*(w)$ to pure tensors. If $F(e_i\otimes1)=\sum_j w_j\otimes a_{ji}$, send $F$ to $\sum_{j,i}E_{ji}\otimes a_{ji}$. The two composites are identities on these bases and on pure tensors. Thus $j_A$ is an isomorphism for every commutative $k$-algebra $A$. Both its definition and matrix description commute with maps $A\to B$. All sums are finite, including the empty sums when either space is zero.

source.place: Remark 4.1, printed p.84: finite-basis description; explicit elementary Hom base-change calculation

proof.text: Apply [lem-sfb-hopf-coaction-linearization] with $E=k$, with its trivial coaction $a\mapsto a\otimes1$, and $M=V,W$. Both structure maps $E\to L=C$ are the same. The given coactions therefore determine $C$-linear isomorphisms $D_M:M_C\to M_C$, with $D_M(m\otimes c)=\rho_M(m)c$. Their pullbacks to the identity are identities. On $G\times_k G$, write $D_{M,1}$ and $D_{M,2}$ for pullbacks along the first and second projections, and $D_{M,12}$ for pullback along multiplication. The cocycle supplied by the cited statement is $D_{M,12}=D_{M,1}D_{M,2}$. Its inverse formula supplies genuine inverses, without reducedness or testing on field-valued points.

source.place: Tag 03LF, definition-equivariant-module, identity and cocycle; affine coaction-linearization correspondence specialized to the point

proof.text: Use $j_C$ to define a $C$-linear isomorphism $D_H$ on $H_C$ by $j_C(D_H(F))=D_Wj_C(F)D_V^{-1}$. Its inverse is $T\mapsto D_W^{-1}TD_V$ under $j_C$. Its identity pullback is the identity. Naturality of $j_A$ from step 1 identifies all its pullbacks with the same conjugation formula. On $G\times_kG$ the two cocycles from step 2 give, for every matrix $T$ over $C\otimes_k C$, $$D_{H,1}D_{H,2}(T)=D_{W,1}D_{W,2}T D_{V,2}^{-1}D_{V,1}^{-1}=D_{W,12}T D_{V,12}^{-1}=D_{H,12}(T).$$ This is equality over the coordinate algebra, not merely at geometric points. Hence $D_H$ has the required identity and cocycle. Only associativity of composition and $(PQ)^{-1}=Q^{-1}P^{-1}$ were used; the latter is verified by multiplying on both sides.

source.place: Lemma 22.40 (b) to (a), printed p.477: natural Hom action; identity and cocycle expanded explicitly

proof.text: Apply the reverse direction of [lem-sfb-hopf-coaction-linearization], again for $E=k$, now to $M=H$ and the isomorphism $D_H$ just constructed. It gives the coaction $\rho_H(f)=D_H(f\otimes1)$ and proves both its coassociativity and counit identities. For $g\in G(A)$ let $D_M(g)$ denote pullback of $D_M$ along $g:\operatorname{Spec}A\to G$. Pulling the cocycle back to $(g,g^{-1})$ and $(g^{-1},g)$ gives $D_M(g)^{-1}=D_M(g^{-1})$. Pulling back the definition of $D_H$ therefore yields $g\cdot F=D_W(g)FD_V(g^{-1})$, exactly $(g\cdot F)(v)=g\cdot F(g^{-1}\cdot v)$. The cocycle and identity also give $D_M(gh)=D_M(g)D_M(h)$ and $D_M(1)=1$, so these are precisely the actions induced by the coactions.

source.place: Remark 4.1, printed p.84, universal-element recovery of the coaction; Lemma 22.40, p.477, Hom action

proof.text: For $f\in H$, put $f_C=f\otimes_k C$. By construction $\rho_H(f)=f\otimes1$ is equivalent, under $j_C$, to $D_W f_C D_V^{-1}=f_C$, hence to $D_W f_C=f_C D_V$. The morphism clause of [lem-sfb-hopf-coaction-linearization] identifies the last equality with $\rho_W f=(f\otimes1)\rho_V$. Alternatively, restrict it to $v\otimes1$ to get that equation directly, and extend $C$-linearly for its converse. Pullback gives $D_W(g)f_A=f_AD_V(g)$ for every $A,g$, which is the asserted equivariance. Conversely, assume this equality for every $A,g$. Take $A=C$ and the universal point $g=\operatorname{id}_G\in G(C)$ (the morphism $\operatorname{Spec}C=G\to G$). The equality becomes $D_Wf_C=f_CD_V$, proving the reverse implication even for a nonreduced group scheme.

source.place: Remark 4.1, printed p.84, universal element; Lemma 22.40 (b) to (a), printed p.477, fixed maps are G-homomorphisms
